facts.text: On this date in 1321, Dante Alighieri died in Ravenna — a city he'd fled to in exile, having been sentenced to death by his native Florence. He never returned, and Florence only formally apologized in 2008.
On this date in 1812, Napoleon entered Moscow to find it largely abandoned and on fire — set ablaze by Russians themselves. He held the city for 35 days and gained nothing.
More people live within a 4,000 km radius centered on Bangladesh than outside it — roughly half of all humanity clustered in one of Earth's least-celebrated corners.
Vatican City has a lower average age than any country on Earth, despite its population being almost entirely elderly clergy. The math is distorted by constant turnover of young Swiss Guards.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, containing roughly 60% of the world's fresh surface water — yet faces no particular global reputation as a water power.
On this day in 1971, Nixon's price controls froze wages and prices across the entire U.S. economy — a market intervention so sweeping it briefly made America feel more Soviet than capitalist.
On Sept 14, 2008, Lehman Brothers' board voted to file for bankruptcy, triggering the largest Chapter 11 filing in U.S. history: $613 billion in debt, gone by morning.
The NYSE was founded under a buttonwood tree in 1792 by 24 brokers who agreed to charge each other lower commissions — Wall Street began, essentially, as a price-fixing cartel.
Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6 billion in a single day, yet the company sold less than 2% of itself. It remains the most profitable business in human history.
Berkshire Hathaway's Class A shares have never been split. One share cost roughly $19 in 1965; today it trades above $700,000 — Buffett kept the price high to discourage short-term traders.
On this date in 1959, Luna 2 became the first human-made object to reach another world, crashing into the Moon at 3.3 km/s — 12 years before Apollo astronauts landed softly.
On September 14, 1752, Britain went to sleep on the 2nd and woke on the 14th. Parliament skipped 11 days to adopt the Gregorian calendar, and people rioted demanding their days back.
Your skeleton is not the rigid scaffold it feels like. Bone is constantly being dissolved and rebuilt, replacing itself entirely every 10 years through a cellular demolition crew called osteoclasts.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly 10 million tons on Earth.
Mantis shrimp see with 16 types of photoreceptors — humans have 3 — yet research shows they are worse at distinguishing similar colors. Evolution built them to identify, not compare.
On this date in 1812, Napoleon entered a burning, abandoned Moscow — a city set ablaze by Russians rather than surrendered. He waited 35 days for a peace offer that never came.
The fax machine was patented in 1843, making it older than the telephone, the light bulb, and the American Civil War.
On this date in 1901, President McKinley died from his gunshot wound — killed not by the bullet, but by physicians probing it with unwashed fingers.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid is that old.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Europe's oldest university predates the civilization Cortés would later destroy.
Saudade (Portuguese): a melancholic longing for something beloved and lost. Linguists consider it untranslatable because it mourns the absence of things that may never have existed at all.
Hiraeth (Welsh): homesickness for a home you cannot return to — or never had. The word folds grief, longing, and incompleteness into a single breath.
On this date in 1321, Dante Alighieri died in Ravenna. The word 'inferno,' now generic for any hell, entered English almost entirely because of him.
Vellichor: coined by writer John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, it names the strange wistfulness of a used bookshop — proof that invented words can feel ancient.
Petrichor, named on this date's seasonal cusp as autumn nears, was coined only in 1964. It blends the Greek for stone and ichor, the fluid in the veins of gods.
On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared ICOs illegal and ordered exchanges to shut down — Bitcoin dropped 20% within days, then recovered to all-time highs within weeks.
On this date in 2022, Ethereum completed The Merge, switching from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and cutting its energy consumption by roughly 99.95% overnight.
Bitcoin's genesis block contains the text 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — both a timestamp and a pointed editorial comment embedded permanently on-chain.
The DAO hack of 2016 didn't exploit a flaw in Ethereum — it exploited a flaw in one smart contract. The hard fork that followed was a political choice, not a technical necessity.
Satoshi Nakamoto's known wallet addresses hold roughly 1.1 million BTC that have never moved — making them simultaneously the most-watched and most-irrelevant addresses in crypto market structure.

On this date in 2009, ImageNet launched publicly — the dataset that made deep learning's dominance inevitable. Without its 14 million labeled images, the 2012 AlexNet moment likely arrives years later, if at all.

On this date in 1956, the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was wrapping up — the meeting that coined the term 'AI' and set expectations the field would spend decades failing to meet.

GPT-4 was trained on roughly 50 petaflop/s-days of compute. The human brain runs its entire lifetime on approximately 100 watts — the two are not comparable in any simple way, which is exactly the point.
Transformers have no built-in notion of sequence order. Positional encodings are a patch, added by hand, to compensate for an architecture that is otherwise entirely order-blind.

AlphaFold2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known protein universe — yet determining why many of those structures fold the way they do remains unsolved biology.
